text:
For a circular orbit, the geometric transit probability is approximately

\[
P_{\rm tr}\simeq \frac{R_\star}{a}.
\]

Using Kepler’s third law,

\[
a\propto (M_\star P^2)^{1/3}.
\]

Given \(P_1=P_2/3\) and \(M_1=2M_2\),

\[
\frac{a_1}{a_2}
=\left[\frac{M_1}{M_2}\left(\frac{P_1}{P_2}\right)^2\right]^{1/3}
=\left[2\left(\frac13\right)^2\right]^{1/3}
=\left(\frac{2}{9}\right)^{1/3}.
\]

Since both stars have the same radius,

\[
\frac{P_{\rm tr,1}}{P_{\rm tr,2}}
=\frac{a_2}{a_1}
=\left(\frac{9}{2}\right)^{1/3}
\approx 1.65.
\]

Thus, Planet 1 has about 1.65 times the transit probability of Planet 2.

Answer: D
